headline: Corals show El Niño is now 40 percent stronger

sources.title: 'This is such a clear story': Climate change is supercharging El Niño to unprecedented strengths, study finds (Live Science)

chunks.text: El Niño is a natural [[climate pattern]] where part of the Pacific Ocean {{heats up}} every few years, changing weather worldwide. Researchers led by Julia Cole of the University of Michigan found that El Niño events of the last 40 years were about 40 percent stronger than in the [[preindustrial era]], and stronger than any in a [[record]] that {{goes back}} roughly 1,000 years. The study {{came out}} in the [[journal]] Science on August 27, 2026.

verbs.why: A parked car heats up fast in the summer sun, and a kitchen heats up when the oven is on. El Niño happens when part of the Pacific Ocean heats up every few years, changing weather around the world.

verbs.correct: To reach far into the past
verbs.why: A family's story can go back five generations, and some town records go back hundreds of years. The coral record in this study goes back roughly 1,000 years, and recent El Niño events are stronger than anything in it.
A new phone comes out every fall, and a popular book can come out in twenty languages. This study came out in the journal Science on August 27, 2026.

chunks.text: The team {{carried out}} a study of 13 Galápagos corals, including living corals and ancient [[boulders]]. Corals {{build up}} [[growth bands]] over time, like tree rings. They drilled [[cores]] and measured [[chemical signals]] in the skeleton that change with water temperature. From these they {{worked out}} [[sea-surface temperatures]] for the last 1,000 years. They then compared the results with [[climate models]] of natural causes, such as [[volcanic eruptions]] and changes in the sun, to {{rule out}} those explanations.

verbs.wrong: To continue doing the same thing
verbs.why: A hospital can carry out a survey of its patients, and a mechanic carries out a full check of a car. The team carried out a study of 13 corals from the Galápagos Islands, including living corals and ancient coral boulders.

verbs.correct: To form slowly in layers over time
verbs.wrong: To be the parts that form a whole
verbs.why: Dust builds up on a shelf nobody cleans, and ice builds up on a plane's wings in cold weather. Corals build up growth bands over time, much like the rings of a tree.

verbs.wrong: To describe results in a formal report
verbs.why: A detective works out who was in the room from a few clues, and a shopper works out the total before reaching the register. The researchers worked out sea-surface temperatures for the last 1,000 years from chemical signals in the coral skeletons.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not the cause
verbs.wrong: To choose one thing for special study
verbs.why: A doctor can rule out an infection with a simple test, and police rule out a suspect who was out of town. The team compared its results with climate models to rule out volcanic eruptions and changes in the sun as the cause.

chunks.text: In the 1,000-year record, the strongest recent events {{stand out}}. "This is such a clear story," Cole said. "The big El Niño events of the last 40 years are not normal in the context of the last thousand years." The rise in [[intensity]] {{lines up with}} global warming since the [[widespread]] use of [[fossil fuels]] began in the 1800s. Since natural causes cannot explain it, the change {{comes down to}} human-caused warming, they say. Several other universities took part.

verbs.correct: To be clearly different from the rest
verbs.wrong: To give the same result when tested again
verbs.why: A red coat stands out in a gray crowd, and one great player stands out on a weak team. In the 1,000-year record, the strongest recent El Niño events stand out clearly.

verbs.wrong: To be as good as expected
verbs.why: A witness's story should line up with the video, and a receipt should line up with what you actually bought. The rise in El Niño intensity lines up with the rise in global temperatures since fossil fuel use began in the 19th century.

verbs.correct: To have something as the real cause
verbs.wrong: To become sick with an illness
verbs.why: A close game often comes down to one last shot, and a hard choice usually comes down to money. With natural causes ruled out, the researchers say the change comes down to human-caused warming.

chunks.text: Stronger El Niño events can {{set off}} [[droughts]], floods, and [[wildfires]] worldwide. They are also linked to [[food insecurity]], damage to homes and roads, and conditions in which diseases such as cholera {{break out}}. They could also cause [[lasting shifts]] in major [[ecosystems]] such as the Amazon rainforest. Meanwhile, global temperatures are on a path that could {{end up}} 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.

verbs.wrong: To keep something for later use
verbs.why: A piece of burnt toast can set off a smoke alarm, and one rumor can set off a panic. Stronger El Niño events can set off droughts, floods, and wildfires in different parts of the world.

verbs.correct: To start suddenly, as a disease does
verbs.wrong: To stop working because of damage
verbs.why: A fire can break out in an old kitchen, and a fight can break out at a crowded game. Strong El Niño events create conditions in which diseases such as cholera break out.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a level or state
verbs.wrong: To stop rising and stay the same
verbs.why: A late train can end up an hour behind schedule, and a small loan can end up costing twice its size. Global average temperatures are on a path that could end up 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.

mainIdea.s: Scientists used 1,000 years of Galápagos coral records to measure past ocean temperatures. They found recent El Niño events are far stronger than before, and human-caused warming explains it.
mainIdea.why: Coral cores from the Galápagos gave 1,000 years of sea-surface temperatures, and El Niño events of the last 40 years are about 40 percent stronger than in the preindustrial era.

mainIdea.s: Coral records show El Niño has grown about 40 percent stronger in recent decades. Researchers say natural cycles, such as volcanic eruptions and the sun, explain most of the increase.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the researchers compared the record with models of natural causes and ruled them out. They say the change comes down to human-caused warming.

mainIdea.s: A survey found reefs in the eastern Pacific lost half their living coral during a recent marine heat wave. Scientists say warmer water is making it much harder for the damaged reefs to recover.
mainIdea.why: There was no survey of reef damage and no marine heat wave. The corals were used as a 1,000-year temperature record to measure El Niño strength.

tf.s: Stronger El Niño events can set off droughts, floods, and wildfires.
tf.why: They are also linked to food insecurity, damage to homes and roads, and outbreaks of diseases such as cholera.

tf.s: The coral record the team used goes back only about 100 years.
tf.why: The record goes back roughly 1,000 years, and the El Niño events of the last 40 years are stronger than anything in it.

tf.s: Chemical signals in the coral skeletons revealed past ocean temperatures.
tf.why: The researchers worked out sea-surface temperatures for the last 1,000 years from signals in the skeletons that change with the temperature of the water.

tf.s: The researchers blame changes in the sun for the stronger El Niño events.
tf.why: Natural causes such as the sun and volcanoes could not explain the pattern, so the researchers say the change comes down to human-caused warming.

tf.s: The study came out in the journal Science on August 27, 2026.
tf.why: Julia Cole of the University of Michigan led the study, with scientists from several other universities.

tf.s: The team found that volcanic eruptions caused the stronger El Niño events.
tf.why: Climate models were used to rule out volcanic eruptions and changes in the sun as the cause, not to show that they caused anything.

lines.text: Did you see the El Niño study that {{came out}} last week?
The coral one? I saw the headline. Forty percent stronger, right?
Right. Over the last 40 years, El Niño events have been about 40 percent stronger than before the industrial age. [[Let that sink in]].
That's a big jump. But how do you measure El Niño from a coral? [[Walk me through it]].
They drilled cores from corals in the Galápagos. The corals {{build up}} bands every year, like tree rings, and the chemistry of each band changes with the water temperature.
So the coral is keeping a temperature diary.
Exactly. From those signals they {{worked out}} sea-surface temperatures for a record that {{goes back}} about a thousand years.
A thousand years. [[No wonder]] the recent events {{stand out}}.
The lead researcher, Julia Cole, said the big events of the last 40 years are simply not normal in that context.
Couldn't it just be volcanoes or the sun?
They ran climate models to {{rule out}} natural causes. The increase {{lines up with}} the warming from fossil fuels since the 1800s.
So it {{comes down to}} us. [[Case closed]].
In her words, "This is such a clear story." And stronger events can {{set off}} droughts, floods, and wildfires around the world.
[[Not exactly comforting]]. And where do temperatures {{end up}} on the current path?
Somewhere around 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels. [[The writing is on the wall]].
